topic: Caffeine: adenosine blocking, half-life, sleep loss, crash, withdrawal
hook: What coffee really does to your brain
caption:
Your morning coffee doesn't give you energy. It blocks the signal that tells your brain you're tired. Caffeine fits into the same receptors as adenosine, the molecule that builds sleep pressure all day.

That's why the effect lasts so long. On average, half your caffeine is still in your blood around 5 hours after your cup. A late coffee can quietly cut your sleep even if you fall asleep fine.

How many cups do you drink a day? Be honest 👇

1/5 It hijacks sleep signals
Caffeine looks like adenosine, the molecule that makes you sleepy, and blocks its receptors in your brain.

2/5 Half stays for hours (5 hrs)
On average, half the caffeine from your cup is still in your blood about 5 hours later.
📷 massage-techniques (CC BY-SA 2.0) via wikimedia

3/5 It steals your sleep (-1 hr)
In one study, a strong dose taken 6 hours before bed still cut total sleep by more than an hour.
🎨 AI-generated image

4/5 Why the crash hits
Adenosine keeps piling up while it's blocked. When caffeine fades, it floods the receptors at once.
🎨 AI-generated image

5/5 Your brain adapts (24 h)
Daily drinkers may grow extra adenosine receptors. Skip a day and withdrawal headaches can start within 12 to 24 hours.
